about.label: About Me
about.p1: I'm Mohamed Khalil, a front-end developer from Egypt. I build with React, JavaScript, TypeScript, and CSS. Most of my focus goes into making interfaces that work well on any screen and don't get in the user's way.
about.p2: I completed the DEPI React Front-End Developer track and built several projects along the way: an e-commerce app, a weather app, and DevFolio. Honestly, I learned more from debugging those than from any course.
about.p3: Since January 2026 I've been a front-end intern at CASCOTEC, working on iCasco, a certification management platform built with React, Vite and TypeScript, with full Arabic/English (RTL/LTR) support. I've built pages from scratch, written the form-validation logic, turned Figma mobile designs into reusable components, and audited the platform's 22 API endpoints.

ecommerce.idea: I wanted a project that goes beyond static pages: accounts, a cart that survives navigation, and a real checkout flow. An online store forces you to solve what every serious front-end app faces — authentication, shared state, private pages, forms and a REST API. The data comes from a public practice API, so no real orders are placed.
ecommerce.role: Solo project. I planned the screens, routes and state, wrote all of the React code, styled it and deployed it.

challenges.title: A cart count that is always right
challenges.body: The cart badge in the navbar has to match the cart page, even after adding a product from another page. Instead of passing counts around, I put every cart action in one CartContext. Add, update, remove and load all read the item count from the API response and update the shared state, so the badge changes in exactly one place.

challenges.title: A token that was always one step behind
challenges.body: After signing in, adding to the cart failed until the page was refreshed. The cart code read the saved token once, when its file loaded, so every request after login still carried the empty one. The token is now read at the moment each request is sent, and the cart provider reloads the count whenever the login state changes.

challenges.title: Keeping private pages private
challenges.body: Cart, orders and checkout must not open for a signed-out visitor. I wrapped those routes in a ProtectedRoutes component that reads the login state from context, so logging out sends the visitor to the sign-in page immediately, and the rule is written once instead of in every page.

challenges.title: Everything that can fail on a network call
challenges.body: Early on, a failed request left a blank page or crashed a screen, for example when a session expired. Every call now rejects on failure and each screen shows a readable message with a Try again button, and the sign-in form shows the API's own error text.

challenges.title: Brands from a paginated API
challenges.body: The brands endpoint returns data page by page. I loop until the last page, then run the search box and the A–Z filter in the browser, so filtering feels instant.

decisions.title: React 19, Vite and React Router 7
decisions.body: Vite gives instant feedback while building. The router's nested layouts let the navbar and footer exist once, while sign-in and sign-up use their own layout.

decisions.title: Context API instead of Redux
decisions.body: Only two things are truly global here: the signed-in user and the cart. Context covers that without another library. I would reach for a state library only if the app grew.

decisions.title: Formik and Yup for forms
decisions.body: Sign-up, sign-in and checkout need clear validation messages. Formik tracks values and touched fields, and Yup keeps the rules in a readable schema.

decisions.title: A hosted payment page
decisions.body: Checkout collects the shipping details and sends the visitor to the payment page created by the API, so card details never pass through my code. The return address is the site's own origin, so it works wherever the app is deployed.

decisions.title: Load heavy pages on demand
decisions.body: Products, cart, checkout, orders, brands and the auth pages are loaded with React.lazy, which cut the first download from about 675 kB to about 555 kB of JavaScript.

outcome: A complete shopping flow: sign up, sign in, browse and search products, view details, manage the cart, check out and see your real orders.
Every screen that calls the API has loading and error states, with a way to try again.
Real data only: I removed fake discounts, placeholder order history and buttons that did nothing, so what the screen shows is what the API returned.
A responsive layout built on Bootstrap's grid, with a CSS module for every component.
Live and deployed, with the code public on GitHub.
ecommerce.learned: A project is not finished when the happy path works. When I reviewed it the way a client would, I found a stale token, a payment return address hard-coded to localhost, error cases that crashed screens, and placeholder data presented as real. Fixing those taught me more than building the first version did. Next I would add TanStack Query for caching and tests for the cart logic, and I would write it in TypeScript, which I started using after this project.

velora.idea: Velora is a landing page for a fictional premium organic coffee brand. I wanted to practice what makes a marketing page feel alive (storytelling sections, product cards, motion on scroll) and to do it in Arabic, fully right-to-left, with HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript. The products, prices, reviews and numbers are sample content, and the page says so.
velora.role: Solo project: layout, Arabic copy, styling and all the JavaScript, with no framework. I later reviewed and cleaned it up before featuring it.

challenges.title: Designing for right-to-left
challenges.body: The page is Arabic from the root: <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">. Setting the direction once on the root element made text and layout flow right-to-left, and I then checked every section for spacing, icons and slider direction instead of patching them one by one.

challenges.title: Many scroll animations, one pattern
challenges.body: Each section reveals itself when it enters the screen. I used IntersectionObserver rather than scroll listeners, and one small helper adds the animation class to every block. The classes are added by JavaScript, so if the script fails the whole page is still visible, and reveals are skipped for visitors who prefer reduced motion.

challenges.title: Honest demo behaviour
challenges.body: A first version had buttons and a newsletter form that did nothing. I replaced the dead links with real section anchors and made the cart buttons and the form show a clear message that this is a demo and nothing is sent or stored.

decisions.title: No framework
decisions.body: A brand landing page has no complex state. Plain JavaScript keeps it light and let me practice the browser APIs underneath frameworks.

decisions.title: Bootstrap 5 for the grid
decisions.body: I used it for the responsive grid and the navbar and wrote the visual identity (colours, cards, hero) in my own CSS.

decisions.title: Swiper, hosted locally
decisions.body: A touch-friendly slider with clickable pagination. I serve it from the repo instead of a CDN, pause autoplay on hover and turn it off for reduced motion.

outcome: A seven-section responsive Arabic landing page: hero, story, products, features, testimonials, call to action and footer.
Scroll reveals, animated counters, a scroll-spy navbar that closes on mobile after a tap, and a testimonials slider. The page passes an automated axe accessibility check.
Live on GitHub Pages with the code public.
velora.learned: This project taught me how much work lives in the details of animation timing and RTL, and that a demo should never pretend to be a real shop: dead buttons and invented numbers hurt trust, so unfinished parts are now labelled instead of left looking real.

qr.idea: A one-screen demo landing page, built to practice a polished first impression: a bold hero, subtle depth, and an endless strip of partner logos. The company names are fictional and the page is labelled as sample content.
qr.role: Solo project: design, HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

challenges.title: A seamless logo marquee
challenges.body: The partner strip scrolls forever with no visible jump. The logos are duplicated and the track moves by exactly half of its width, so the loop restarts invisibly. It pauses on hover, soft fades on both edges hide where logos enter and leave, and the duplicate half is hidden from screen readers.

challenges.title: Depth without heaviness
challenges.body: The hero content drifts slightly slower than the scroll for a parallax feel, using a passive scroll listener throttled with requestAnimationFrame. Sections fade up once through IntersectionObserver.

challenges.title: A bug I found in review
challenges.body: The page loaded its script from the wrong path, so the parallax and fade-ups silently never ran. Checking the network panel in a real browser run showed the 404. Fixing the path was one line, but it taught me to test the deployed behaviour and not only how it looks.

decisions.title: CSS for motion, JavaScript only where needed
decisions.body: The marquee and hero entrance are CSS animations, which the browser can run smoothly. JavaScript only decides when something becomes visible.

decisions.title: Content stays visible without JavaScript
decisions.body: The reveal classes are added by the script, so the page is fully readable if it fails. All motion also stops for visitors who prefer reduced motion.

outcome: A focused landing page with a hero entrance, parallax, scroll reveals and an infinite marquee.
Responsive on phone, tablet and desktop, with no horizontal overflow, and no accessibility violations in an automated axe check.
Live on Vercel with the code public.
qr.learned: Small, well-timed animation does more for perceived quality than many effects, and a missing file can hide behind a page that still looks fine. Next time I would test the live page in a browser console before calling it done, and compress the logo images further.

alex.idea: A dark portfolio template for a back-end developer, built to practise layout, CSS modules and small interactions. The challenge was to make a back-end profile feel visual, so the hero types out a real API route as if you were watching the code being written. All the content (the name, companies, numbers and projects) is made-up sample data, and the page says so.
alex.role: Solo project: structure, design, content layout and all the React code.

challenges.title: A typing animation without a pile of linked state
challenges.body: The hero code is typed one character at a time with a blinking cursor. A single tick counter drives everything: how many lines are visible and how much of the current line is typed are calculated from it, so there is one timer to start and clean up. With prefers-reduced-motion the finished code appears at once, and the decorative editor is hidden from screen readers.

challenges.title: Filterable projects
challenges.body: Visitors can filter the project list by category. The filter is derived from a single piece of state and the list, so there is no duplicated data to keep in sync.

challenges.title: Sample content that cannot be mistaken for real
challenges.body: The template shows a made-up engineer with made-up employers. Instead of leaving that to guesswork, the page carries a dismissible Demo template notice, the project cards say Sample project, the company names are fictional, and the only real contact details are mine. Buttons with nowhere real to go were removed rather than left pointing at #.

decisions.title: Sections as components
decisions.body: Hero, About, Experience, Tech Stack, Projects and Contact are separate components with their own CSS modules, so each part can change without touching the others.

decisions.title: Content kept as data
decisions.body: Projects, stats and tech tags live in arrays at the top of each file, so filling the template with real details is an edit to data, not to markup.

decisions.title: Remove what does not work
decisions.body: The contact form only logged to the console, so I removed it instead of shipping a button that does nothing. Unused packages and a duplicate font import went with it.

outcome: A responsive one-page template with a typing hero, floating technology tags, an experience timeline, a tech stack, filterable projects and a contact section.
No automated accessibility violations (axe) on desktop and mobile, no horizontal scrolling, and motion switched off for visitors who ask for it.
Live on Vercel with the code public. The profile content is sample content for the design.
alex.learned: Animation timers are easy to get subtly wrong in React, and one derived counter is easier to reason about than several linked pieces of state. I also learned to be explicit about demo content, because a convincing fake profile can be mistaken for a real one. Next time I would add TypeScript types for the content arrays.

weather.idea: A weather app I built during DEPI to practise HTML, CSS, JavaScript and working with a real API. It shows today's conditions and the next two days for any city, using WeatherAPI. After the first version worked I rewrote it for reliability: a search that does not hammer the API, honest error states, and a layout that works with a keyboard.
weather.role: Solo project: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, API integration, and the later rewrite for reliability and accessibility.

challenges.title: Search that fires on every keystroke
challenges.body: The first version requested a full forecast for every letter typed after the third. That wastes the API quota, and a slow response for "Alex" could arrive after the one for "Alexandria" and overwrite it. Typing now only fetches suggestions, debounced by 300 ms, and every request cancels the previous one with AbortController, so the latest request always wins.

challenges.title: Everything that can go wrong with a network call
challenges.body: A city that does not exist, a lost connection, a slow server and an exhausted quota all used to leave the page frozen on the previous result. Requests now time out after 10 seconds, WeatherAPI error codes map to plain-language messages with a Try again button, and when the network fails the app shows the last saved forecast for that city with a clear warning.

challenges.title: An API key that ended up on GitHub
challenges.body: The first version had the key written straight into the script and pushed to a public repository. I moved it into a config file that is not committed, generate that file from an environment variable in the Vercel build step, and rotated the exposed key. The main lesson is that any key used in browser JavaScript is visible to visitors, so a front-end key must be low-value and replaceable.

challenges.title: Dates that showed the wrong weekday
challenges.body: Parsing a date-only string such as 2026-10-11 with new Date() treats it as UTC, so viewers west of UTC could see the previous day. The forecast date already belongs to the city, so it is now formatted as-is, without shifting it by the viewer's time zone.

decisions.title: Shape the API response before rendering
decisions.body: The raw payload is validated and reduced to a small model with only the fields the UI uses. If something is missing, the app reports a readable error instead of crashing halfway through updating the screen.

decisions.title: Write API text with textContent, never innerHTML
decisions.body: City names and conditions come from an external service, so they are inserted as plain text. Icon URLs are only accepted from WeatherAPI's own CDN, with a local fallback icon if one fails to load.

decisions.title: Both units from one response
decisions.body: WeatherAPI returns Celsius and Fahrenheit together, so switching units only re-renders the data already on the page. The choice and the last city are remembered between visits.

decisions.title: Ask for location only when the user taps the button
decisions.body: A permission prompt on page load is intrusive and easy to dismiss by reflex. The Use my location button asks at the moment the user wants it, and a denial shows a clear message and leaves search available.

outcome: A working three-day forecast with live suggestions, a °C/°F toggle and remembered settings.
Reliable under failure: timeouts, cancelled stale requests, readable errors and a saved-forecast fallback.
Keyboard-operable search (combobox pattern), labelled controls, visible focus and reduced-motion support.
The background image went from 12.6 MB to 354 KB, and the page no longer loads Font Awesome or Google Fonts.
Live on Vercel with the code public.
weather.learned: Most of the work in a small API app is not the happy path, it is cancelled requests, error messages and bad data. Next I would add unit tests for the data-shaping and formatting functions, and put the API key behind a tiny serverless proxy so it is not exposed to the browser at all.
